body:
Two moduli, one hidden relation

We know two curve points, \(P\) and \(Q=[d]P\), and want the hidden scalar \(d\). Point multiples repeat modulo the order \(r\) of \(P\), while their coordinates use a different prime \(p\). The curve equation below defines those coordinates; the quantum algorithm extracts a relation between scalar labels.

\[ E:\ y^2=x^3+7\pmod p,\qquad p=2^{256}-(2^{32}+977). \]

Evaluate \(f(k,l)=[k]P+[l]Q=[k+dl]P\). Different pairs \((k,l)\) can produce the same point whenever \(k+dl\) agrees modulo \(r\). That is the useful structure: equality of outputs groups the input labels along a direction determined by the secret.

What the three register labels mean

We use two input registers for \(k,l\) and an accumulator \(A\) for the point. To see the Fourier relation cleanly, first imagine labels in \(\mathbb Z_r\). The physical qubit registers instead have \(m\) bits and contain labels from 0 to \(2^m-1\), with \(m\) chosen relative to \(n=\lceil\log_2r\rceil\).

LabelMathematical valueStorage in the logical arithmetic circuit
\(k,l\)Binary integers whose point multiples depend only on their residue modulo \(r\)Two \(m\)-qubit scalar registers in the clean theoretical circuit. The implementation later measures and reuses small window registers.
\(A\)One curve pointTwo field-element registers, \(A=(x_A,y_A)\), each containing 256 logical qubits. Fault-tolerant encoding stores the logical qubits collectively in larger physical code blocks. “One point register” therefore bundles two coordinate registers. This is the chosen affine representation, not an information-theoretic lower bound on storing a point.

The ideal accumulator begins at the identity \(\mathcal O\). The implementation starts at a known random nonzero point and shifts the lookup tables. This avoids identity entries and distributes the remaining exceptional additions. The final constant translation affects only the point register, leaving the input Fourier statistics unchanged.

A line becomes a Fourier constraint

Suppose the point register has value \([c]P\). The compatible inputs satisfy \(k=c-dl\), so they form a uniform line of labels. Apply the inverse Fourier transform to both inputs, using \(F_r|a\rangle=r^{-1/2}\sum_u e^{2\pi iau/r}|u\rangle\). The transform turns that line into a constraint on measured frequencies.

For general order \(r\): why only one frequency line survives

The state below shows this conversion explicitly. Conditioning on the point makes the line visible in the derivation; measuring the point is optional because tracing it out gives the same input statistics.

\[ |\psi_c\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_l|c-dl,l\rangle \xrightarrow{F_r^\dagger\otimes F_r^\dagger} \frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_u e^{-2\pi icu/r}|u,du\rangle. \]

At frequency pair \((u,v)\), the terms along the line contribute \(\sum_l e^{2\pi il(du-v)/r}\). They add when \(v=du\) and cancel otherwise. The offset \(c\) contributes only a phase. Thus a nonzero \(u\) lets us recover \(d=vu^{-1}\pmod r\).

Qubits broaden the peaks

A qubit register has size \(M=2^m\), so its finite lines do not fit the group period exactly. Their Fourier peaks broaden. Another way to describe the same process is two phase estimates of commuting translations by \(P\) and \(Q\). They share a uniformly sampled eigenlabel \(s\), with phases \[ \theta_1=s/r,\qquad \theta_2=(ds\bmod r)/r. \]

With enough precision, rounding the two estimates recovers their integer numerators and hence the secret. Mosca's bound quantifies this event. Ekerå's search uses nearby candidates to recover additional samples and accommodate shorter controls.

First do the computation classically

We next need a circuit for the point-valued function. Begin classically: divide each scalar into windows of \(w\) bits, \[k=\sum_i k_i2^{iw},\qquad l=\sum_i l_i2^{iw},\qquad 0\le k_i,l_i<2^w.\] Each digit chooses one precomputed multiple of \(P\) or \(Q\). The position of the window determines the table, and its digit determines the row.

For each position \(i\), compute the tables \[T_i^{(P)}[j]=[j2^{iw}]P,\qquad T_i^{(Q)}[j]=[j2^{iw}]Q.\] before the quantum run. The schedule knows \(i\); only the row address is quantum. This replaces many bit-controlled point additions by one table selection and one addition per window.

Every entry is a known coordinate pair. Computing multiples of the public point \(Q\) does not require knowing \(d\). The two-bit example below shows the first few tables explicitly, so we can follow how their place values combine.

Address jWindow 0: T₀[j]Window 1: T₁[j]
0\(\mathcal O\)\(\mathcal O\)
1\(P\)\([4]P\)
2\([2]P\)\([8]P\)
3\([3]P\)\([12]P\)

For \(k=11=3+4\cdot2\), use row 3 of the first table and row 2 of the second. The accumulator goes from \(\mathcal O\) to \([3]P\), then to \([11]P\). Applying the same procedure to \(l\) and the Q tables produces \([k]P+[l]Q\). The actual 16-bit tables each have 65,536 rows.

The example uses unshifted tables for clarity. In the implementation, each table receives a known offset \(R_i\) chosen to exclude \(\mathcal O\), and the accumulator starts at \(A_0\ne\mathcal O\). All outputs acquire the same translation \(A_0+\sum_iR_i\). This preserves the Fourier relation while the failure analysis accounts for the remaining exceptional additions.

What one accumulator update computes

One update adds two points, \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\). On the nonexceptional branch, compute their slope and then the new coordinates: \[\lambda=(y_1-y_2)(x_1-x_2)^{-1},\qquad x_3=\lambda^2-x_1-x_2,\qquad y_3=\lambda(x_2-x_3)-y_2.\] These formulas identify the required arithmetic: field division, square subtraction, and multiplication.

Field division is where gcd enters. Euclid gives \(a\Delta x+bp=1\), making \(a\) the inverse of the nonzero coordinate difference. The paper applies that inverse through recorded reductions. The point-addition lesson then arranges the formulas so temporary values can be cleared without revealing the selected address.

Now make the lookup coherent

Now promote the row address to a \(w\)-qubit register. The table remains classical data compiled into gates. If \(F_i(j)\) is the coordinate bit string for row \(j\), load it by XOR into a target register: \[L_i:|j\rangle|z\rangle\longmapsto |j\rangle|z\oplus F_i(j)\rangle.\] This operation preserves the address and is reversible for every initial target value.

Starting the target at zero loads the selected word. Applying the same XOR lookup again clears it. On a superposition of addresses, linearity gives \[\sum_j\alpha_j|j\rangle|0\rangle\longmapsto\sum_j\alpha_j|j\rangle|F_i(j)\rangle.\] This is a coherent lookup, not the point addition itself: the latter acts on the loaded coordinates afterward.

The lookup never asks a classical processor to read the address. Each basis branch follows its corresponding table row, so the address and output can become entangled while preserving the interference needed by the algorithm.

Inside the lookup: a complete two-bit example

The next diagram exposes every gate for a two-bit address and a two-bit output word \(f_1f_0\). It is a small data table chosen to illustrate lookup mechanics; the full coordinate word has 512 bits.

Address j₁j₀Stored word f₁f₀Output bits to flip
0001z₀
0110z₁
1011z₁ and z₀
1100None

For address 10, only the final two gates fire and write 11. In a superposition, the same gate sequence applies the appropriate row to every branch. Starting from an arbitrary output \(z\) produces \(z\oplus f(j)\), which also shows why the circuit is reversible.

How this scales to a long coordinate word

For a long output word, repeatedly testing the full address for each output bit wastes work. Compute the row selector \(a=[j=t]\) once, use it to flip every 1 in the constant row, then clear it. The selector's cost is shared across the entire word.

Unary lookup also shares partial address tests between neighboring rows. The compiler overlaps two such traversals in its zipper schedule. Both changes preserve the XOR contract. The diagram shows compute–copy–uncompute; measurement with phase repair can replace part of the cleanup.

The shared-test circuit behind unary lookup

At one node of the traversal, let \(c\) enable the subtree and \(x\) choose its branch. Compute \(a=cx\) and use it to load word \(D_1\). A CNOT changes it to \(c(1-x)\), enabling \(D_0\). Restore the AND value, then erase it by X measurement and conditional CZ. One AND has served both branches and every output bit.

The full lookup sequence expands this node into an eight-entry table, then into the two controlled 15-bit traversals used by the paper. It also shows the block relays and phase repair needed when coordinate outputs are cleared.

Use the loaded point, then clear it

With lookup available, the following circuit loads a point, adds it to the accumulator, and clears the loaded word. Each point wire contains two coordinate registers. This gives the logical construction before optimizing when its workspace is released.

The optimized addition loads coordinates three times because their workspace is needed between uses. The first lookup forms coordinate differences; the second supplies \(3x_2\) for square subtraction; the third removes the final offsets. X measurements free each output early and a later phase lookup repairs their signs. The cleanup circuit follows this reuse explicitly.

ChangeWhat it savesWhat it costs
16-bit windowsOne addition per window\(2^{16}\)-entry lookups
Direct first lookupThe first additionA separately charged initialization
Omit three windowsThree more additions; 28 remainClassical recovery of 48 missing bits
Measure and reuse controlsTwo persistent scalar registersAdaptive Fourier rotations and feedforward

The conservative Fourier branch adds one control bit per scalar, making the initial direct lookup contain \(2^{18}\) entries. Later windows remain 16 bits. Once a window has been used and Fourier-measured, its controls can be reset while the point accumulator stays coherent.

title: III. From an elliptic-curve key to a Fourier sample

body:
The headline combines different claims

A useful attempt must do three things: produce a recoverable Fourier sample, compute its oracle accurately enough, and survive the physical execution. These are different probabilities. Keeping them separate explains how the paper arrives at 63.3% and 40.7% for recovery of \(d\) from \(Q=[d]P\).

Ideal recovery

Start with \(P_0\), the success probability of Fourier sampling and classical recovery with an exact oracle.

Approximate arithmetic

Next bound \(p_f\), the probability that a fixed oracle input encounters a wrong value or phase under fresh randomization.

Physical execution

Finally multiply by hardware survival \(1-L\), where \(L\) is the modeled probability of a logical fault during the attempt.

The separate confidence level \(1-2^{-128}\) applies to the sampled arithmetic bound. It describes confidence in an upper bound on failure, not the success probability of an attempt. We now follow how that bound changes the Fourier calculation.

Wrong phases count as wrong answers

Consider clearing a computed work bit \(b(x)\) by X measurement. Although its measured qubit is released, the input branch acquires a sign depending on the readout \(m\). If the repair is wrong, interference changes even when the numerical oracle output is correct.

For fixed randomness \(\omega\), put every input label with a wrong output or residual minus sign into \(B_\omega\). The guarantee needed by the proof is pointwise: for each \(x=(k,l)\), fresh masks and cleanup outcomes make it bad with probability at most \(p_f\).

\[ \forall x:\quad\Pr_\omega(x\in B_\omega)\le p_f. \]

The X-readout amplitude is \(2^{-1/2}(-1)^{mb(x)}\). Its magnitude does not depend on the input, so each readout is uniform even conditional on previous outcomes. Its sign still matters, which is why cleanup outcomes belong in the randomized failure analysis.

A Z error takes \(|+\rangle\) to \(|-\rangle\) without changing its computational-basis probabilities. A following Hadamard turns those states into opposite outcomes, \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\).

The masked oracle also translates its point output by a known amount. Imagine undoing that translation only for the proof. It permutes the output register and leaves the control statistics unchanged, allowing every ideal randomized run to be compared with the same state \(|\Psi\rangle\).

Randomization gives a linear amplitude penalty

The result is a bound on averaged recovery probability \(\widetilde P\). It subtracts an error from the ideal success amplitude, then squares. When identifying a bad branch, include any uncleared workspace as part of the output state.

\[ \boxed{\widetilde P\ge\bigl(\max\{0,\sqrt{P_0}-2p_f\}\bigr)^2.} \]

The amplitude penalty is linear in \(p_f\). The reason is that the failure guarantee holds separately for every input label: we can average each label's error over the masks before taking its norm.

Proof: average, bound, project

For \(N\) equally weighted labels, write the mean state error as \(\Delta=N^{-1/2}\sum_x|x\rangle|d_x\rangle\). A good branch contributes zero. A bad branch contributes the difference of two unit vectors, of norm at most 2. Averaging that contribution gives the first inequality below; orthogonality of the input labels gives the second.

\[ \|d_x\|\le2\Pr_\omega(x\in B_\omega)\le2p_f, \qquad \|\Delta\|^2=\frac1N\sum_x\|d_x\|^2\le4p_f^2. \]

Let \(M\) project onto successful Fourier-and-recovery outcomes, expressed before the Fourier transform. It is independent of the random seed. Jensen's inequality bounds the actual average probability by the projected mean ket, and the reverse triangle inequality bounds its distance from ideal success.

\[ \mathbb E_\omega\|M\widetilde\Psi_\omega\|^2 \ge\|M\mathbb E_\omega\widetilde\Psi_\omega\|^2 \ge\bigl(\max\{0,\sqrt{P_0}-\|\Delta\|\}\bigr)^2. \]

The physical experiment averages probabilities over random runs. The mean ket is an intermediate mathematical object used to lower-bound that average. This distinction is exactly what the first inequality expresses.

For a tight example, flip one uniformly chosen sign in an N-term uniform state. Each label is wrong with probability \(1/N\), while projection back onto the uniform state succeeds with \((1-2/N)^2\).

Two routes to the reported probabilities

Appendix B obtains \(p_f\le0.03346\). The main-text calculation rounds it upward to 0.0335 and applies the same amplitude formula to the two exact-oracle baselines, giving the numbers in the table.

Ideal baselineAfter arithmeticAfter modeled hardware
Mosca: \(0.6570\)\((\sqrt{0.6570}-0.067)^2\approx0.553\)\(0.553\times0.7355\approx40.7\%\)
Ekerå heuristic: \(0.99\)\((\sqrt{0.99}-0.067)^2\approx0.861\)\(0.861\times0.7355\approx63.3\%\)

The conservative baseline uses sufficient phase precision and requires classical search to cover the ambiguity from the omitted 48 bits. The 99% baseline uses Ekerå's heuristic recovery estimate. Applying the arithmetic inequality preserves those starting assumptions. Hardware survival is then included under the assumption that the no-logical-fault branch follows the stated algorithmic distribution.

What one attempt buys

A candidate is checked by computing \([d]P\) and comparing with \(Q\). Independent attempts with success \(s\) succeed by attempt \(m\) with probability \(1-(1-s)^m\). The 25.7-day figure times one quantum attempt; classical recovery cutoffs and a full runtime benchmark for the omitted bits remain part of the Limitations.

title: IV. What does a 63% success probability mean?

body:
Approximation is paid for in success probability

The arithmetic saves gates by stopping some carries and comparisons early. We need to know how often those shortcuts change the coherent computation. Appendix B answers this for the noiseless logical circuit before physical errors are introduced.

A failure includes a wrong residue, a noncanonical output, an unrepaired phase, or nonzero scratch at deallocation. The bound holds for every fixed scalar input, averaged over fresh masks and uniform X-measurement outcomes. Here the field prime is \(p=2^{256}-(2^{32}+977)\), and the curve-group order is \(r\).

Randomize

Random offsets make a fixed scalar input explore the sets on which arithmetic can fail.

Count

Following the ideal calculation lets us count where the first failure could occur.

Transfer

A union bound combines those events and supplies the input to the Fourier-success inequality.

Reversibility adds an exceptional point

Adding a fixed point \(C\) is reversible as a group operation. The chosen affine-coordinate formulas have exceptional inputs, listed below, where a denominator vanishes.

OperationDivision usedExceptional input \(A\)
Compute slope\((y_A-y_C)/(x_A-x_C)\)\(C,-C\), or nonaffine \(\mathcal O\)
Erase slope from output\((y_C+y_{A+C})/(x_C-x_{A+C})\)\(\mathcal O,-2C\)

The extra case \(A=-2C\) comes from cleanup. Its sum is \(-C\), which shares C's x-coordinate, so the denominator needed to remove the slope is zero. Reversibility therefore adds an exception beyond the forward slope calculation.

The initial accumulator is uniform over nonidentity points, and each table shift is random over its allowed choices. For a fixed digit, the selected entry ranges over \(r-2^w\) points, with \(w=16\). Along an ideal trajectory, reaching \(\mathcal O\) was already an earlier exception. Three new bad offsets per step therefore give the bound below, where \(L=\lceil n/w\rceil=16\).

\[ p_{\rm exception}\le\frac{6L}{r-1},\qquad L=\lceil n/w\rceil=16. \]

Short carries can lose values

Next consider modular reduction. Overflow past bit \(n\) should be replaced by a short addition of \(c\), since \(2^n\equiv c\pmod p\). The implementation limits that correction to \(\kappa\) low bits. Later, \(\delta\) will denote comparison width and \(\rho\) carry padding.

Write an integer sum as \(u=q_u2^n+r_u\), with one overflow bit \(q_u\) and low word \(r_u\). Assuming \(2c\le2^\kappa\le2^n\), the correction behaves as follows. If adding \(c\) escapes its window, the indicator \(w_u\) is 1 and the result loses \(2^\kappa\). If no overflow occurs, values in \([p,2^n)\) instead remain noncanonical.

\[ \operatorname{red}_\kappa(u)=r_u+q_uc-q_uw_u2^\kappa, \quad w_u=1[(r_u\bmod2^\kappa)\ge2^\kappa-c]. \]
BoundaryFailure mechanism
\(p\le u<2^n\)No overflow: the result stays noncanonical.
\(q_u=w_u=1\)The correction carry escapes: the result loses \(2^\kappa\).

Short comparisons can lose phases

A different shortcut can affect only phase. Erasing work bit \(b(x)\) by X measurement produces \((-1)^{mb(x)}\). If the repair uses a cheaper predicate \(\widetilde b(x)\), the remaining sign is

\[ (-1)^{m(b(x)\oplus\widetilde b(x))}. \]

A disagreement can therefore change Fourier interference while leaving every output bit correct. The failure count includes each such disagreement, even when a particular measurement outcome would produce no residual sign.

Transfer field counts to curve probabilities

We first count bad pairs of canonical field inputs. Missed reduction, escaped carry, and incorrect phase comparison give the bound \(N_{\rm add}\) below. We then transfer that count to curve-coordinate inputs by counting how many point pairs produce each field pair. Write \(D=(r-1)(r-2^w)\).

The addition count and its factor 10 \[ N_{\rm add}\le 2^{n-1}c\left(1+\frac{p-2c-1}{2^\kappa}\right) +\frac{(2^{n-\delta}-1)(p-c)}2. \]

For the three masked additions, a field pair has at most \(4p\), \(2(r-1)\), and \(4p\) preimages respectively. Divide by the \(pD\) equally likely mask choices. Since \(r-1<p\) for secp256k1, the result is \(p_{\rm add}\le10N_{\rm add}/D\), already covering all three additions.

Subtraction surrounds addition by the complement \(C(v)=p-1-v\). Its truncated implementation fails on \(N_{\rm cmpl}=c(2^{n-\kappa}-1)\) inputs. The four subtraction sites have coordinate multiplicities 4, 9, 9, and 4, leading to the combined bound below.

\[ p_{\rm sub}\le\frac{26N_{\rm sub}}D \le\frac{26(N_{\rm add}+2pN_{\rm cmpl})}D <1.05938\times10^{-8}. \]

Negation computes \(p-u\), then exchanges the encodings 0 and \(p\). With \(\kappa=65\) and a 32-bit zero test, its carry and comparison failures give \(p_{\rm neg}<6.9850\times10^{-10}\). The addition bound at \(\kappa=65,\delta=32\) is \(p_{\rm add}<1.74623\times10^{-9}\).

A mask makes a carry count useful

For square subtraction, add a uniform mask to the target before applying \(y\leftarrow y-x^2\). This makes the target uniform for each fixed \(x\), so counting bad carry and comparison values gives a probability bound. Removing the mask afterward restores the desired operation.

Failure siteConstraint on a uniform targetCount in the square
Local carryCross all \(\rho\) padding bits\(16\cdot2^{-\rho}\)
Wrapping correctionOverflow the \(\kappa\)-bit correction\((9+2\cdot13)c2^{-\kappa}\)
Phase repairEqual high \(\delta\) bits, or noncanonical target\(9\cdot2^{-\delta}+9c2^{-256}\)
\[ p_{\rm sq}\le(1+c/p)\left(16\,2^{-\rho}+35c\,2^{-\kappa} +9\,2^{-\delta}+9c\,2^{-256}\right)<9.89531\times10^{-9}. \]

The displayed value uses \(\rho=\delta=32\) and \(\kappa=65\). The integer squares and their exact auxiliary correction computations introduce no approximation. The counted failures arise in target updates and phase cleanup.

The dominant term is measured, then bounded

The gcd circuit uses a different source of evidence: simulations of its finite iteration and register budgets. Let \(q_{\rm div}\) and \(q_{\rm mul}\) be its true failure probabilities on uniform field inputs. A statistical upper bound on them must first be obtained, then transferred to the actual curve inputs.

The paper tests one million uniform pairs \((u,v)\in\mathbb F_p^*\times\mathbb F_p\) in each direction. Both multiplication and division produce 21 failures. The observed frequency, the confidence bound, and the approximate curve multiplicity factor are displayed separately below.

Observed rate\[21/10^6=0.000021\]
One-sided upper bound\[q_U=0.000149304\]
Curve-input transfer\[p_{\rm gcd}\lesssim4(q_{\rm div}+q_{\rm mul})\]

The Clopper–Pearson bound chooses \(q_U\) so that \(\Pr_{q_U}[K\le21]=2^{-129}\). Combining the two directions gives confidence at least \(1-2^{-128}\). Reproducing the bound requires the same rounded schedule and counts of phase and scratch failures as well as wrong outputs.

Why the factor is approximately four

Why is the curve multiplicity at most four? Fix coordinate differences \(u\ne0,v\). Subtracting the two curve equations gives \(2vy+v^2=3ux^2+3u^2x+u^3\). For \(v\ne0\), eliminate \(y\) to obtain the quartic below.

\[ (3ux^2+3u^2x+u^3-v^2)^2-4v^2(x^3+7)=0. \]

A quartic has at most four roots, each fixing a point. If \(v=0\), at most two x-coordinates each allow two y-coordinates, again giving four. The output-side slope multiplication has the same property. This yields the transfer inequality below.

\[ p_{\rm gcd,div}+p_{\rm gcd,mul} \le\frac{4p(p-1)}D(q_{\rm div}+q_{\rm mul}). \]

Count first failures; no independence is needed

Count the first failure along the ideal trajectory and sum over sites; independence between sites is unnecessary. One addition has \(p_{\rm ecadd}\le0.001195\). Almost all comes from the gcd term, approximately \(8q_U=0.001194432\); the remaining arithmetic contributes about \(2.29\times10^{-8}\). Across 28 additions, include the exceptional-point bound to obtain

\[ p_f\le28p_{\rm ecadd}+\frac{6L}{r-1}\le0.03346. \]

This pointwise randomized bound gives \(\widetilde P\ge(\max\{0,\sqrt{P_0}-2p_f\})^2\). The amplitude proof explains that final step. Physical logical faults enter only after this logical-circuit analysis.
summary: Short carries and comparisons save gates. Random masks let their bad inputs be counted and converted into a bound on the coherent algorithm.
title: Appendix B. Every way the arithmetic can fail

body:
The algorithmic structure IonQ inherits

A curve point can be easy to add and hard to label. Given \(P\) and \(Q=[d]P\), we can compute more multiples of either point, but the scalar \(d\) remains hidden. The group has known prime order \(r\); its coordinate calculations use the field prime \(p\).

Shor's algorithm converts this hidden label into a Fourier relation. Proos and Zalka explain how to implement the required oracle using reversible elliptic-curve arithmetic over prime fields. IonQ keeps that algorithmic structure and changes the arithmetic and its physical realization.

Abstractly, the generated group is \(\mathbb Z_r\). Computationally, we are given coordinates for \([a]P\), not the label \(a\). The task is precisely to recover that hidden labeling. The function below exposes a relation without requiring us to invert the coordinate map.

The secret is a direction, not an output

The oracle can be unchanged while its two scalar inputs move. One such direction depends on d, so identifying that direction identifies the secret.

\[ f(k,l)=[k]P+[l]Q, \quad f(k+r,l)=f(k,l),\quad f(k+d,l-1)=f(k,l). \]

Equal outputs occur along shifted copies of \(H=\{(-dl,l)\}\). Within one copy, the point register carries no information distinguishing the scalar labels. Those labels can therefore interfere when Fourier-transformed.

Input direction\[(-d,1)\]
Surviving frequency\[(u,v)\cdot(-d,1)=0\]
Recovered scalar\[d=vu^{-1}\pmod r\]

The sum of their phases is \(\sum_l e^{2\pi i(v-du)l/r}\), which cancels unless \(v=du\). For prime \(r\), any measured \(u\ne0\) can be inverted to recover \(d\). Binary control registers replace the exact constraint with peaks around the corresponding frequencies.

Reading the input labels immediately would yield random values and lose this interference. Likewise, leaving temporary data that distinguishes equal-output labels would spoil the Fourier pattern. A correct quantum oracle must produce the point and clear its work coherently.

A permutation needs clean temporary space

Translation by a fixed point is a permutation, with inverse translation by its negative. A generic reversible implementation computes \(F_T(A)=A+T\) into a second register, exchanges the registers, and uses the inverse relation to clear the old point: \[ |A,0\rangle\longmapsto|A,F_T(A)\rangle \longmapsto|F_T(A),A\rangle \longmapsto|F_T(A),0\rangle. \]

The optimized affine circuit reduces that temporary storage by reusing coordinates. To clear its slope, it uses the output coordinates, introducing an additional denominator. At \(A=-2T\), the output is \(-T\), whose x-coordinate equals T's. This explains the extra exceptional input in the reversible construction.

Reversible inversion creates the scheduling problem

The oracle's coordinate division uses an inverse modulo the field prime. Euclid finds it by expressing 1 as a combination of the denominator and the prime.

\[ au+bp=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u^{-1}=a\pmod p. \]

Euclid supplies the field inverse through the identity above. Different denominators take different numbers of steps, so a quantum circuit must preserve the branch decisions and use a common schedule. Measuring when a branch finishes would reveal information about its input.

ChoiceConsequence
Schedule for the worst inputAll branches fit; larger circuit.
Short schedule and shrinking registersLower resources; rare branches fail.
Fresh arithmetic masksSpread those failures over fixed logical inputs.

IonQ uses finite iteration and width budgets and includes their failures in its sampled bound. The inherited contribution is the reversible-arithmetic construction; the new resource totals come from the changed circuit and architecture.

Once a candidate scalar is returned, checking \([d]P=Q\) determines whether it is correct. This makes unsuccessful attempts recognizable. The probability of producing a useful sample is still set by the quantum calculation and classical recovery method.

summary: The secret appears in a relation between inputs that produce the same point. Reversible field arithmetic must preserve that relation without leaving distinguishing workspace.
title: Reference [3, 24]. Why Shor works for elliptic curves

body:
Measure early, preserve the distribution

A Fourier transform followed immediately by measurement does not need to keep all its output qubits coherent. Once one output bit is measured, its remaining controlled phase gates can use that classical result. This is the observation that allows the control register to be reused.

Griffiths and Niu replace those quantum controls by adaptive rotations. The measured distribution is exactly the same, even when the inputs are entangled with another register. Here we use \(F_N|y\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_xe^{2\pi ixy/N}|x\rangle\) and measure after its inverse.

The whole argument is one measurement identity

A measured control has become a classical bit. The controlled gate can be applied to the target afterward using that bit, with the same conditional operation.

\[ C(V)=|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes V, \qquad (\langle m|\otimes I)C(V)=V^m(\langle m|\otimes I). \]

The identity above explains the replacement. Projecting a controlled-V gate onto control result \(m\) leaves \(V^m\) on the target. We may therefore measure the control first and apply V only when the classical result is 1. Equality of measurement operators preserves the behavior on entangled inputs as well.

Quantum controls become classical wires

In the Fourier circuit, the relevant gates are phases \(R_j=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{2\pi i/2^j})\). Their controlled version is symmetric between its wires. Choose the first measured wire as control, move its measurement ahead of the remaining phases, and repeat for the next wire.

A visual check: decode five

The example begins with \(F_8|5\rangle\). Its three wires carry the phases shown below. Each measured bit tells us part of the phase on the next wire, so feedback removes that known part before the next Hadamard and readout.

WireInitial phaseFeedback factorAfter feedbackBit after \(H\)
\(q_2\)\(-1\)\(1\)\(-1\)\(y_0=1\)
\(q_1\)\(i\)\(e^{-\pi i/2}\)\(+1\)\(y_1=0\)
\(q_0\)\(e^{5\pi i/4}\)\(e^{-\pi i/4}\)\(-1\)\(y_2=1\)

The readouts give \(y_0=1,y_1=0,y_2=1\), hence \(y=y_0+2y_1+4y_2=5\). The wire labels already account for the usual Fourier bit reversal.

Cancel the known tail

For a general integer \(y=\sum_h2^hy_h\), step \(j\) reads the next bit from least to most significant. The phase is \(y/2^{j+1}\) turns. Previously measured low bits supply a known fractional tail, canceled by the rotation below.

\[ \phi_j=-2\pi\sum_{h<j}\frac{y_h}{2^{j+1-h}}, \qquad \operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\phi_j}). \]

After cancellation, only the sign \((-1)^{y_j}\) remains, so a Hadamard reveals the next bit. For a phase that is not exactly binary-representable, outcomes are probabilistic. The adaptive circuit still reproduces the full Fourier measurement distribution.

Reuse the controls, retain the accumulator

Phase estimation prepares these control phases through powers of a unitary. If \(|\psi\rangle\) has eigenphase \(\theta\), applying a controlled \(U^{2^j}\) to a fresh \(|+\rangle\) control produces the state below.

\[ |+\rangle|\psi\rangle\xrightarrow{C(U^{2^j})} \frac{|0\rangle+e^{2\pi i2^j\theta}|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}|\psi\rangle. \]

Interleave that preparation with the adaptive readout, then reset the measured control. The same construction works on superpositions of eigenstates with the appropriate conditional work-register updates. IonQ retains a 16-bit window for efficient table lookup, measures it, and reuses it while preserving the curve accumulator.

The saving is in coherent control storage. Classical feedforward and the required accurate rotations still consume time and resources. They enter the compiled schedule and the separate rotation-synthesis error budget.

title: Reference [57]. Measuring the Fourier transform one qubit at a time

body:
Why the conservative baseline is 65.7%

Binary Fourier sampling produces a peak near the desired phase rather than an exact rational label. We want a lower bound on how often the measured value can still be rounded to the right numerator. Begin with an exact oracle for \(Q=[d]P\) in a known prime-order group of order \(r\), and enough control precision.

Mosca's Corollary 19 supplies the bound used for the conservative baseline. Each of two phase estimates has a useful pair of neighboring outcomes with probability at least \(8/\pi^2\), leading to the expression below.

\[ P_0\ge\frac{r-1}{r}\left(\frac8{\pi^2}\right)^2\approx0.6570. \]

Both estimates refer to the same hidden eigenlabel. Recovering their numerators gives that label and its product with \(d\), allowing a modular division to recover the secret.

Two measurements of the same hidden label

Translations by P and Q have common eigenstates. Their two phases contain the same random label, allowing the secret to be recovered by a ratio of numerators.

\[ |\chi_s\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_a e^{-2\pi isa/r}|[a]P\rangle, \quad \theta_1=s/r,\quad\theta_2=(ds\bmod r)/r. \]

Translation by \(P\) has the displayed eigenvectors, with \(a\) running from 0 to \(r-1\). Translation by \(Q\) shares them. Starting from the identity point samples \(s\) uniformly. Conditional on \(s\), the two measurement distributions factor, with phases measured in turns as shown.

Bound a peak, then convert it to an integer

For a control register of size \(M=2^m\), the amplitude at outcome \(z\) is a finite geometric sum. Squaring it gives the peak profile below. This is the quantity we need to bound near its center.

\[ \Pr(z\mid\theta)=\left|\frac1M\sum_{a=0}^{M-1}e^{2\pi ia(\theta-z/M)}\right|^2 =\frac{\sin^2(\pi M(\theta-z/M))}{M^2\sin^2(\pi(\theta-z/M))}. \]

If the phase is exactly representable, its outcome occurs with certainty. Otherwise write \(M\theta=j+\alpha\), with \(0<\alpha<1\). The peak lies between integers \(j\) and \(j+1\), and their respective errors are displayed below.

Left neighbor\[z=j,\quad\text{error}=\alpha/M\]
Hidden phase\[M\theta=j+\alpha\]
Right neighbor\[z=j+1,\quad\text{error}=(1-\alpha)/M\]

Bound both neighboring probabilities by replacing their denominator sines with their arguments, using \(|\sin t|\le|t|\). Adding them gives the inequality below.

\[ \Pr(j)+\Pr(j+1)\ge \frac{\sin^2(\pi\alpha)}{\pi^2}\left(\frac1{\alpha^2}+\frac1{(1-\alpha)^2}\right) \ge\frac8{\pi^2}. \]

The minimum occurs halfway between the two outcomes, at \(\alpha=1/2\). Keeping both neighbors yields \(8/\pi^2\); using only the nearest one would give the weaker \(4/\pi^2\). We must now ensure that both neighbors round to the same group numerator.

One extra bit makes both neighbors useful

The two neighbors are useful only if both identify the correct group numerator. One extra precision bit places each within the required rounding interval.

\[ M\ge2r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |z/M-s/r|<1/M\le1/(2r) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{round}(rz/M)=s. \]

The displayed precision condition does that: after multiplication by \(r\), either neighbor lies within half an integer of the correct numerator. Distances are circular and the answer is modulo \(r\). For an n-bit order, \(M=2^{n+1}\) suffices. IonQ uses this one-bit padding argument instead of Mosca's two padding bits.

With \(r=19,M=64,s=3\), the peak lies between outcomes 10 and 11. Both give \(\operatorname{round}(19z/64)=3\), so either recovers the numerator.

Both estimates are useful with probability at least \((8/\pi^2)^2\). The shared eigenlabel is nonzero with probability \((r-1)/r\); when it is nonzero, compute \(d=(ds\bmod r)s^{-1}\). Multiplying these factors gives approximately 65.7%.

The omitted 48 bits need an additional argument

IonQ also omits 48 control bits and replaces them with classical search. The rounding argument above does not by itself cover that shorter register: the search must resolve its additional ambiguity. The postprocessing lesson derives the recovery equation and identifies the search parameters needed to reproduce this branch.

This establishes the exact-oracle baseline under its precision and recovery assumptions. Approximate arithmetic changes that probability through the amplitude bound; physical survival enters afterward in the full resource estimate.

title: Reference [56]. Deriving the conservative Fourier success bound

body:
Missing quantum bits become classical search

A shorter quantum control register gives a less precise Fourier sample. We can trade that lost precision for classical work by searching nearby candidates and checking them against the public key. The group input is \(P,Q=[d]P\), with known prime order \(r\).

Ekerå develops this tradeoff for binary Fourier sampling. IonQ omits three 16-bit windows and uses a heuristic 99% ideal-recovery estimate. To understand what that means, first derive how a sample yields a candidate, then examine how much probability the chosen search is expected to cover.

Fix the sign and register lengths

Fix the Fourier convention before deriving a candidate. The reference uses a minus sign in the oracle and two independently chosen binary register lengths.

\[ A=2^{m+\varsigma},\quad B=2^\ell,\qquad (a,b)\longmapsto[a]P-[b]Q, \quad0\le a<A,\ 0\le b<B. \]

The equations above use control dimensions \(A=2^{m+\varsigma}\) and \(B=2^\ell\), where \(m\) is the bitlength of \(r\) and \(\varsigma\) is padding. They also use the minus-oracle \([a]P-[b]Q\) and positive-exponent Fourier transforms. Translating from IonQ's plus-oracle requires the corresponding sign change in a measured frequency.

A useful sample has two small corrections

Round the scaled measurement outcomes, then search small corrections to those rounded values. The relation below converts each admissible correction into a candidate scalar.

Round the sample\[z=\operatorname{round}(rj/A),\quad C=\operatorname{round}(rk/B)\]
Search nearby relations\[d(z+\eta)+C=t\pmod r\]
Recover and verify\[d=(t-C)(z+\eta)^{-1}\pmod r\]

Given outcomes \((j,k)\), round the scaled values to \(z,C\), then search the chosen intervals of offsets \(\eta,t\). Each invertible \(z+\eta\) gives a candidate through the displayed equation. Accept it only if \([d]P=Q\).

For example, modulo 19 take \(z=3,C=16\). Zero offsets give candidate 1; trying \(t=-1,\eta=0\) gives \((-1-16)3^{-1}=7\). This demonstrates the candidate calculation, independently of how likely that sample is.
Where the integer relation comes from

The recovery equation comes from the phase of a nearby peak. Let \(\Delta\) be its integer displacement, \(\delta_\eta\in[-1/2,1/2)\) its rounding offset, and \(n_d\) the integer that accounts for modular wrapping. Their relation is

\[ d(z+\eta)+rk/B+n_dr=r(\Delta-\delta_\eta)/B. \]

Rounding passes the integer terms through unchanged. It replaces \(rk/B\) by \(C\) and the right side by \(t=\operatorname{round}(r(\Delta-\delta_\eta)/B)\). Reducing modulo \(r\) removes \(n_dr\), giving the exact candidate equation.

Why 99% is heuristic

To estimate how often a bounded search finds the right candidate, examine the Fourier peak. A length-B control and angular displacement \(\phi\) in radians give the profile below.

\[ h(\phi)=\frac1{B^2}\left|\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}e^{ib\phi}\right|^2 =\frac{\sin^2(B\phi/2)}{B^2\sin^2(\phi/2)}. \]

Its width scales as \(1/B\). Ekerå estimates captured probability by treating distinct peak families separately when \(d/r\) has no unusually good small-denominator rational approximation. The exact distribution includes interference between those families. Numerical integration of the separated-peak approximation supplies the heuristic probability estimate.

A known shift \(Q\mapsto Q+[a]P\) can randomize the secret's label for this distribution argument. After recovery, subtract \(a\). This randomization concerns the Fourier peak model; the arithmetic masks serve a different purpose.

The tradeoff has a square-root search cost

A shorter register widens the possible residual interval. Classical recovery solves the resulting group equation over that interval.

\[ |t|\lesssim \frac r{2^\ell}(B_\Delta+1/2), \qquad [t]P=[C]P+[z+\eta]Q. \]

For an accepted peak displacement bounded by \(B_\Delta\), the residual \(t\) lies in the interval indicated above. Removing one control bit roughly doubles that interval at fixed other settings. For each \(\eta\), recovery is therefore a discrete logarithm over a bounded interval.

Residual intervalDirect candidate searchMeet-in-the-middle scale
\(W\) integers\(W\) trials\(\sqrt W\) stored points and operations
Illustration: \(W=2^{48}\)\(2^{48}\)\(2^{24}\), before constants and peak factors

Baby-step–giant-step searches an interval of width \(W\) in roughly square-root work and storage. Write \(t=a+sb\), with \(s\approx\sqrt W\), store \([a]P\), and match it against \(Q'_\eta-[sb]P\), where \(Q'_\eta=[C]P+[z+\eta]Q\). These are classical search indices and group operations.

What the headline leaves unspecified

The paper does not provide all cutoffs, time–memory choices, and a timed classical implementation for the omitted 48 bits. Its 63.3% result retains the heuristic recovery assumption. A simulator given a known logarithm can test the probability model, but that test does not itself recover an unknown key.
